stories.delivered_paragraph: Elon Musk’s xAI, now owned by SpaceX, sued Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison to block a law targeting apps that generate non-consensual sexualized images. The law, due to take effect Saturday, allows $500,000 fines for each explicit deepfake created; xAI calls it an overbroad, content-based restriction on speech. The suit puts a court at the center of a growing clash between AI-image tools and protections for people depicted without consent.

stories.delivered_paragraph: The Federal Communications Commission announced an import ban covering foreign-made “advanced robotic devices,” including mobile humanoid and quadruped robots, as well as power inverters. The agency cited unspecified “unacceptable risks,” and although it did not name China, the measure will particularly hit Chinese robot makers and inverter suppliers such as Sungrow and already-blacklisted Huawei. The policy could reshape supply chains for robotics and solar-energy equipment while escalating U.S. technology restrictions.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Providence Equity Partners will take full ownership of talent and sports agency THE•TEAM, formerly Wasserman, by buying founder Casey Wasserman’s remaining stake. Providence has been the company’s majority investor since 2022, and president Mike Watt, who assumed day-to-day control after Wasserman announced a sale in February, will become CEO when the deal closes. Financial terms were not disclosed, leaving the agency under a private-equity owner as it transitions beyond its founder.

stories.delivered_paragraph: The Federal Aviation Administration is moving to waive some environmental rules that can slow launch approvals, a step that could benefit companies including SpaceX and Blue Origin. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the administration wants to remove “government red tape” to help the U.S. compete in a new space race. Any change could speed launch licensing, but it also raises questions over how environmental effects near launch sites will be reviewed.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Ari Emanuel backed Paramount’s proposed $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery in a Wall Street Journal opinion article, arguing the deal could help save Hollywood. He dismissed a states’ antitrust lawsuit against the transaction as “trash” and urged regulators to let creative businesses compete. His intervention adds a prominent entertainment-industry voice to the fight over whether combining two major studios and streaming businesses would reduce competition.

stories.delivered_paragraph: The Senate agreed to begin votes on a sanctions package aimed at cutting Russia’s oil revenue and weakening its war effort in Ukraine. Lawmakers combined the Russia measure, named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, with Iran sanctions; it would target purchasers of Russian oil and gas and expand tariff authority. The procedural breakthrough advances a long-delayed congressional effort to pressure Moscow while Ukraine seeks stronger support.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Seattle residents held a candlelight vigil for the three people killed in a gunfight at the Bite of Seattle food festival, where at least four others were wounded. The victims were Junior Cee Niko Semo, 19, Carlos Israel Sanchez Villalba, 44, and Ashley Whitehead, 56; the annual free event typically draws about 350,000 people. Fundraisers and public tributes have focused on families left behind as the city mourns the violence.

stories.delivered_paragraph: President Donald Trump and the Justice Department separately asked the Supreme Court to overturn the $83.3 million defamation verdict won by writer E. Jean Carroll. Trump argues he was immune because his 2019 statements denying her sexual-assault allegation came while he was president, while the DOJ says the government should have replaced him as defendant under the Westfall Act. The appeals test how far presidential and federal-employee protections extend to personal defamation claims.

stories.delivered_paragraph: The Senate confirmed Jay Clayton as President Trump’s director of national intelligence, replacing Bill Pulte, who had served in the role for months after Tulsi Gabbard resigned. Clayton now takes charge of coordinating the U.S. intelligence community and briefing the president on national-security threats. The confirmation ends an extended interim arrangement at a post central to intelligence policy and oversight.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Iran launched a surprise ballistic-missile attack on U.S. forces in the Middle East, but U.S. Central Command said every missile was intercepted. Centcom said the attack originated from Iran, without providing details on the target, damage or casualties. The interception prevented an immediate reported loss, but the episode underscores the risk of a wider confrontation involving U.S. forces in the region.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Netflix narrowly surpassed the BBC as the first place UK viewers say they turn when choosing something to watch, according to Ofcom’s Media Nations report. In 2025, 26% chose Netflix first versus 25% for the BBC, though Ofcom said methodology changes make year-to-year comparisons only indicative; among 16- to 24-year-olds, Netflix led 36% to 14%. The shift increases pressure on the BBC as it renegotiates its funding model.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Ariana Grande sued unidentified hackers in Los Angeles, seeking to identify people she alleges stole and leaked unreleased music, videos and photos. Her complaint says 45 unreleased songs alone were hacked and leaked in 2023, part of hundreds of alleged leaks since her 2011 debut, and accuses the defendants of selling and posting material online. The case seeks to stop distribution and hold those behind persistent entertainment-industry leaks accountable.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” is set to pass the $330 million domestic lifetime total of “Oppenheimer” after only 13 days in theaters, Deadline reported. Its second Monday brought in $14.7 million, with Tuesday projected to exceed $16 million, compared with the 595 days “Oppenheimer” needed to reach its final U.S. total. The unusually strong weekday performance signals sustained demand for the epic rather than a front-loaded opening.

stories.delivered_paragraph: UEFA will hold an emergency meeting to consider responses, including a possible World Cup boycott, to a FIFA plan to sell equity to outside investors, ESPN reported. FIFA is seeking to raise $20 billion through the proposed investment, according to the report. A boycott remains only a possibility, but the dispute exposes a serious rift over how football’s biggest global tournament should be financed and controlled.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Ford raised its 2026 earnings outlook after reporting adjusted second-quarter earnings of 42 cents a share, above the 35 cents Wall Street expected, sending its stock up nearly 7% after hours. It now forecasts adjusted EBIT of $10 billion to $11 billion, citing operational improvements, resilient pricing and profitable vehicle mix despite automotive revenue of $44.89 billion missing estimates. The upgrade signals Ford expects stronger pickup and core-vehicle performance to offset a softer top line.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Seagate reported June-quarter results above Wall Street expectations, and its shares rose after hours, offering investors a positive data point for the battered AI trade. The reaction suggests investors remain willing to reward companies showing that AI-related infrastructure demand is translating into earnings.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Ford’s stock jumped after the automaker leaned on pickup trucks and other traditionally powered vehicles to limit its sales decline, a strategy that aligns it with a key strength at rival General Motors. Investors appeared to welcome the focus on core products, especially as Ford works to stabilize earnings and recover F-Series production.

stories.delivered_paragraph: Micron’s shares were heading toward their worst monthly decline in 11 years as investor concerns grew over China’s expanding domestic supply of chips and chipmaking tools. Analysts said the selloff reflects fears that Chinese competitors could pressure demand or pricing for memory products. The drop highlights how geopolitical competition and shifting supply chains are becoming a material risk even for companies tied to long-term AI demand.
